social.instagram_caption:
Queasy on tirzepatide?

You're not alone — in SURMOUNT-1 (2022), nausea was tirzepatide's most common side effect in adults with obesity (or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes):
- 5mg: 24.6%
- 10mg: 33.3%
- 15mg: 31%
- Placebo: 9.5%
(630–643 people per group)

The catch: it happened mostly while the dose was being stepped up — a trial average, not a prediction for any one person.

Why it happens: tirzepatide slows how fast food leaves your stomach. The FDA label says that effect is biggest after the first dose and eases over time.

Comfort habits that may help:
- Smaller meals, eaten slowly
- Fewer greasy meals
- Sip fluids, unless you've been told to limit them

Red flag: severe belly pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting. The label says stop using it and call your prescriber right away. Vomiting so much you can't keep fluids down? Call your prescriber or get urgent care.

Save this, or share it with someone starting tirzepatide.

factcheck.summary:
The script is accurate and safe to publish. A few minor wording fixes are listed below.

**Checked against sources:**
- **Nausea rates by group (SURMOUNT-1):** 24.6% on 5 mg, 33.3% on 10 mg, 31.0% on 15 mg and 9.5% on placebo. These match the trial and Lilly's results release. The group sizes (630, 636, 630 and 643) match the trial's safety groups.
- **Most common side effect:** stomach side effects were the most common, and they happened mostly while the dose was being increased. This matches the NEJM paper.
- **Why it happens:** the label says tirzepatide slows how fast food leaves the stomach, and that the effect is biggest after the first dose and eases over time.
- **Red flag line:** the Medication Guide says to stop using Zepbound and call your healthcare provider right away for severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting. The script matches this.
- **Habits:** smaller meals, eating slowly, low-fat food and small sips of fluid are all in the Gorgojo-Martínez expert consensus (confirmed on PMC). The Wharton 2022 Postgraduate Medicine paper exists and says the same. The script correctly labels these as expert advice, not trial-tested treatments.

**Framing:**
- Saying "a trial average, not a prediction" avoids overpromising.
- "Unless you've been told to limit them" covers people who have to restrict fluids, such as some people with kidney or heart disease.
- The script includes the line about not stopping or changing medicines, "Not personal advice", and the prescriber line.
- The title's "why it happens and what helps" is fully delivered.

audio.soundNotes: Music sits at -13.5 dB under voice already (good, within -12/-15 target) but drops too low in pauses (-17.6 dB vs ~-14 target), so a modest +1.4 dB (1.15x) lift helps pauses breathe without pushing speech-bed music past -12 dB. SFX cleanup focuses on three problems: a few cues spike well above the -14/-20 dB in-speech ceiling (i16 blip at -6.1 dB, i50 swoosh at -9.2 dB) and are pulled down hard; several clusters stack 5-7 redundant hits inside ~1-1.5s (16.6s, 22.1s, 27.6s, 39.2s, 56.3-57.6s, 61.5s, 86.4s) and are thinned to 3-4 by dropping duplicate ticks/bubbles/pops/blips; and the serious "red flag / stop it / get care" stretch (71.4-82s) gets both thinned and its two entry pops pulled down (~-7.5 dB) so the SFX don't undercut the gravity of that beat, per the dramatic-moment rule. Three bespoke cues (subtle stomach gurgle, a single warm alert chime at the red-flag reveal, and a hopeful closing swell) add texture the stock kit can't give without adding clutter.

hold_reason: Packaging check REVISE: Packaging check (Short): the title, Instagram and Facebook captions match the verified script. They repeat it accurately (24.6/33.3/31/9.5%, 630–643 per group, mostly during dose step-ups, slower stomach emptying biggest after the first dose and easing over time, the red flag, sip fluids unless told to limit them). Every field ends on the disclaimer plus the prescriber line. There is no body shaming, no restrictive-eating nudge and no dosing advice. The blocking issue: the narration ends "Full breakdown: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Side Effects and What Helps, on our channel", but YouTube description line 1 says "Follow for more." with no URL. This is the same funnel/CTA mismatch flagged on 4 earlier Shorts. Minor fixes: Threads doesn't say "don't stop or change your medicines on your own" next to its "label says stop" red-flag line, and it runs about 450 characters against the ~300 target. TikTok writes "weight condition" instead of "weight-related condition", reshapes the step-up claim, and leaves out the don't-stop line. Instagram and Facebook drop the 72-week timeframe from their numbers. I opened no sources, because no packaging claim goes beyond the verified content.
